The early life stages of the Blacknose silverside are characterized by a notably short embryonic period. Eggs incubated at a stable 27 °C [T = 27 °C] complete development and hatch after only 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration that aligns with the rapid embryogenesis observed in other atherinopsids from warm, shallow lacustrine environments. At the moment of eclosion, the prolarvae emerge with a minimal wet weight at birth of just 0.0021 grams [Wwb = 0.0021 grams], a value reflecting the small diameter of the yolk-laden egg. This lecithotrophic alevin then relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. The small size of the newly hatched larva imposes a high surface-area-to-volume ratio, which likely increases the risk of starvation if suitable planktonic prey is not encountered within a narrow window following the yolk-sac resorption. Field observations suggest that this early vulnerability is partially offset by spawning during periods of peak zooplankton abundance in the species' native lacustrine habitats. The transition to exotrophic feeding therefore represents a critical bottleneck in the recruitment process for this species.

Size at the onset of sexual maturation provides important demographic context for understanding the reproductive biology of this species. Individuals first attain sexual maturity at a total length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], a value that represents a considerable proportion of the species' maximum recorded length. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 19 grams [Wwp = approximately 19 grams], a mass that must be achieved before the onset of gametogenesis and the first spawning event. These size thresholds are relatively modest compared to those of larger atherinopsid congeners, reflecting a life-history strategy oriented toward early reproductive output. Once puberty is reached, gonadal development proceeds steadily; the gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 13.9% [GSI = approximately 13.9%] at a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C].

At the upper end of the size spectrum, the Blacknose silverside achieves a maximum recorded total length of 31.7 cm [Li = 31.7 cm], a value derived from studies of congeners and adjusted for morphological differences in body proportions. This ultimate total length corresponds to an asymptotic wet weight of 366 grams [Wwi = 366 grams], representing the largest body mass an individual can attain under favorable environmental conditions. The relationship between length and weight in this species follows a typical fish growth pattern, where mass scales approximately as the cube of length, with a slight exponent exceeding 3.0 indicating a tendency toward relative deepening of the body as the fish grows larger. Such an ultimate body size places this species among the mid-range of the Atherinopsidae, neither among the smallest silversides nor approaching the larger marine relatives. Interestingly, the ultimate length is reached considerably later in life than the length at puberty, a pattern common in many teleosts, indicating that a substantial period of somatic growth follows the onset of reproductive maturity.

Longevity data for the Blacknose silverside, though limited, indicate a relatively compressed lifespan for a fish of its ultimate size. The maximum recorded lifespan under natural conditions is estimated at 8 years [am = 8 years], a figure that has been observed in populations inhabiting moderately warm waters of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This lifespan is relatively brief when compared to longer-lived atherinopsids such as the jacksmelt, but it aligns with the general pattern that smaller-bodied, faster-growing silversides tend to have shorter generation times. The mortality schedule appears to be largely driven by predation pressure from larger piscivorous fish and birds, as well as by periodic fluctuations in water temperature and oxygen availability in their shallow lake habitats. Following the completion of the lifespan, senescence in this species is characterized by a gradual decline in feeding efficiency and a reduced capacity to withstand environmental stressors. Field records indicate that very few individuals survive beyond their eighth year, and those that do show clear signs of physiological deterioration.

Comparative life-history analysis reveals an interesting trade-off between early maturation and ultimate body size. The total length at puberty of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm] represents roughly 38% of the ultimate total length of 31.7 cm [Li = 31.7 cm], a proportion typical of species that invest relatively early in reproduction. This strategy is further reflected in the life expectancy, as the 8-year longevity (8 years) [am = 8 years] observed in natural populations constrains the reproductive window over the adult lifetime at a temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. At a water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth was 14 days [ab = 14 days], and the gonadosomatic index was approximately 13.9% [GSI = approximately 13.9%]. Lower water temperatures would substantially prolong the incubation period and potentially reduce the proportion of body mass directed toward gonadal tissue. Collectively, these life-history traits paint a picture of a species adapted to warm, productive lacustrine environments where rapid early growth and early reproduction are favored over extreme longevity or delayed maturity.
